An Effective Version of Kronecker’s Theorem on the Splitting of Polynomials and the pp-Curvature Conjecture for First-Order Differential Equations

Florian Fürnsinn    Lucas Pannier
Abstract

We develop an effective version of Kronecker’s Theorem on the splitting of polynomials, based on asymptotic arguments proposed by the Chudnovsky brothers, coming from Hermite-Padé approximation. In conjunction with Honda’s proof of the pp-curvature conjecture for first-order equations with polynomial coefficients we use this to deduce an effective version of the Grothendieck pp-curvature conjecture for first-order equations. More precisely, we bound the number of primes for which the pp-curvature of a given differential equation has to vanish in terms of the height and the degree of the coefficients, in order to conclude it has a non-zero algebraic solution. Using this approach, we describe an algorithm that decides algebraicity of solutions of first-order differential equations using pp-curvatures, and report on an implementation in SageMath.

††footnotetext: MSC 2020 classification: 34M15 (primary); 11Y05, 11Y16, 68W30 (secondary)

1 Introduction

A power series f⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[\![x]\!] is called algebraic if there exists a non-zero polynomial P⁡(x,y)∈ℚ⁡[x,y]P(x,y)\in\mathbb{Q}[x,y], such that P⁡(x,f⁡(x))=0P(x,f(x))=0. It is a well-known fact, already known to Abel, that every algebraic power series satisfies a linear differential equation

an​(x)​y(n)​(x)+an−1​(x)​y(n−1)​(x)+…+a1​(x)​y′​(x)+a0​(x)​y​(x)=0a_{n}(x)y^{(n)}(x)+a_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}(x)+\ldots+a_{1}(x)y^{\prime}(x)+a_{0}(x)y(x)=0 (1)

with polynomial coefficients ai​(x)∈ℚ​[x]a_{i}(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x] for i=0,…,n.i=0,\ldots,n.

Conversely, deciding whether the solutions of (1) are algebraic is an old problem dating back at least to Fuchs, and Liouville. More precisely, given (1), one might ask, if

  • (A)

    all solutions are algebraic,

  • (E)

    there exists at least one non-zero solution that is algebraic, or

  • (P)

    a particular solution, given for instance by enough coefficients of its power series expansion such that it is uniquely determined, is algebraic.

Notably, in his paper from 1980 that popularized the study of D-finite series, i.e., power series that satisfy non-zero differential equations of the form (1), Stanley asked for an ‘‘algorithm suitable for computer implementation’’ for problem (P) [47].

Problem (A) was solved algorithmically in a seminal paper by Singer [46], relying on an algorithmic answer of Risch [39] in the case of first order differential equations with algebraic power series coefficients instead of polynomials – this instance of the problem is known as Abel’s problem – and on work conducted by Painlevé and Boulanger [38, 10]. However, this answer is not fully satisfactory, as the complexity of the algorithm involves exponential bounds, making it in general not suitable for implementation. Recent progress on Stanley’s question about problem (P) was made by Bostan, Salvy and Singer [8], giving (semi-) algorithms that rely on the minimization of differential operators annihilating a given D-finite series.

A different – arithmetic – approach to problem (A) was proposed by Grothendieck, in his pp-curvature conjecture [23]. Given (1), we can pass to a matrix differential equation Y′​(x)=A⁡(x)​Y​(x)Y^{\prime}(x)=A(x)Y(x) of order 11, with A⁡(x)∈ℚ​(x)n×nA(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x)^{n\times n} being the companion matrix of (1). Let pp be a prime number. The pp-curvature of the equation is defined as the 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)-linear map ψA:𝔽p(x)n→𝔽p(x)n,Y(x)↦(∂−Ap)pY(x)\psi_{A}:\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n},Y(x)\mapsto(\partial-A_{p})^{p}Y(x), where Ap​(x)∈𝔽p​(x)n×nA_{p}(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)^{n\times n} denotes the reduction of A⁡(x)A(x) modulo pp. The pp-curvature conjecture then states that (1) admits a basis of algebraic solutions if and only if its pp-curvature vanishes for almost all, i.e., all but finitely many, prime numbers pp. Cartier’s Lemma (as attributed by Katz [23]), asserts that the vanishing of the pp-curvature is equivalent to the existence of a full basis of (algebraic) solutions of the reduction of the differential equation modulo pp in 𝔽p​[[x]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![x]\!]. Thus, the pp-curvature conjecture can be seen as a local-global principle about the existence of algebraic solutions of a linear differential equation.

While in general wide open, the pp-curvature conjecture is solved in many cases. Most notably, for ‘‘equations coming from geometry’’, i.e., suitable factors of Picard-Fuchs differential operators, a proof was given by Katz [23], and for hypergeometric differential equations an elementary proof is a by-product of the classification of algebraic hypergeometric functions [3, 15]. For first order equations

y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) (2)

with u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x) the three problems (A), (E) and (P) are equivalent, as there is only a one dimensional solution space of the equation. Honda [18] provided an elementary proof of the pp-curvature conjecture in this case, by showing that the problem is equivalent to a number theoretic result by Kronecker [25], which nowadays is often seen as a consequence of Chebotarev’s Density Theorem [53, 52, 49].

Theorem 1.1 (Kronecker).

Let R⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[x]R(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x] be an irreducible polynomial. If for almost all prime numbers pp, the reduction of R⁡(x)R(x) modulo pp has a root in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, then R⁡(x)R(x) has a root in ℚ\mathbb{Q}, hence R⁡(x)R(x) is linear.

For first order equations with algebraic power series coefficients, i.e., for the equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) with u​(x)∈ℚ¯​[[x]]∩ℚ⁡(x)¯u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[\![x]\!]\cap\overline{\mathbb{Q}(x)}, a proof of the pp-curvature conjecture was given by the Chudnovsky brothers [11]. They use Hermite-Padé approximation to obtain their result. As a motivating example, they apply their methods to provide a new proof of Kronecker’s Theorem, not relying on Chebotarev’s Density Theorem, and in doing so giving also a new proof of Honda’s Theorem.

The pp-curvature conjecture, as stated here, does not provide a way to decide whether (1) has a basis of algebraic solutions, as it translates the statement to a statement about almost all, in particular, a statement about infinitely many, prime numbers. In 1982 Katz extended the pp-curvature conjecture to a conjecture about the Lie algebra of the differential Galois group of a differential equation [24]. From his work presented in [24, §9] it follows by a noetherianity argument that - in the cases in which his conjecture is true, among them first-order equations with rational function coefficients - there exists a finite set of prime numbers, such that the vanishing of the pp-curvatures modulo these primes implies algebraicity of the solutions. However, his argument is non-constructive. The purpose of this article is to explicitly construct a set of primes, for which it suffices to check the vanishing of the pp-curvatures of a first order equation (2) – the cardinality of the set depending on a suitable measure of the ‘‘size’’ of u⁡(x)u(x) – to conclude that it has a non-zero algebraic solution. Our first main result is the following effective version of Kronecker’s Theorem.

Theorem 1.2.

Let

R⁡(w)=rn​wn+…+r1​w+r0∈ℤ⁡[w]R(w)=r_{n}w^{n}+\ldots+r_{1}w+r_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}[w]

be a polynomial with leading coefficient rn>0r_{n}>0, let ΔR≔resw⁡(R0​(w),R0′​(w))\Delta_{R}\coloneqq\res_{w}(R_{0}(w),R_{0}^{\prime}(w)), where R0​(w)R_{0}(w) denotes the square-free part of R⁡(w)R(w), and suppose that the maximal modulus of its complex roots is bounded by B∈ℝB\in\mathbb{R}. Let δ⁡(ΔR)≔∏p|ΔRp1/(p−1)\delta(\Delta_{R})\coloneqq\prod_{p|\Delta_{R}}p^{1/(p-1)} and set M≔⌈2.826⋅rn3⋅δ​(ΔR)3⌉M\coloneqq\left\lceil 2.826\cdot r_{n}^{3}\cdot\delta(\Delta_{R})^{3}\right\rceil and N≔⌈6.076⋅B​M⌉N\coloneqq\lceil 6.076\cdot BM\rceil. Then R⁡(w)R(w) splits into linear factors in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w] if and only if its reduction modulo any prime number pp not dividing rnr_{n} and less than σ≔(2​M+1)​N+2​M\sigma\coloneqq(2M+1)N+2M splits into linear factors in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w].

Our proof of this result makes the Chudnovskys’ proof of Kronecker’s result more explicit. The method of Hermite-Padé approximation inherently is effective in some sense, and in the conclusion of their article [11], the Chudnovsky brothers also claim that their results are effective. However most of their computations are sketched without many details, preventing us from directly deriving explicit bounds. Our contribution is to confirm their claim and to work out concrete bounds.

With this we obtain as a corollary the following method of deciding algebraicity of solutions of first-order differential equations.

Theorem 1.3.

Let u⁡(x)=c⋅a⁡(x)b⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)=c\cdot\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\in\mathbb{Q}(x) be a rational function with a⁡(x),b⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]a(x),b(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] primitive11 1 Recall that a polynomial a⁡(x)=an​xn+…+a1​x+a0∈ℤ⁡[x]a(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\ldots+a_{1}x+a_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}[x] is called primitive, if gcd⁡{a0,…,an}=1\gcd\{a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}\}=1., and c∈ℚc\in\mathbb{Q}. Assume that the coefficients of a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x) are bounded in absolute value by HH. Let

R⁡(w)≔resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))=rn​wn+…+r1​w+r0R(w)\coloneqq\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x))=r_{n}w^{n}+\ldots+r_{1}w+r_{0}

and let Δb≔|resx⁡(b⁡(x),b′​(x))|=|rn|\Delta_{b}\coloneqq|\res_{x}(b(x),b^{\prime}(x))|=|r_{n}|. If b⁡(x)b(x) is square-free and deg⁡b⁡(x)>deg⁡a⁡(x)\deg b(x)>\deg a(x) then, with the notation as in Theorem 1.2, the equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) has a non-zero algebraic solution if and only if its pp-curvatures vanish for all primes not dividing Δb\Delta_{b} and smaller than σ\sigma. Otherwise, no non-zero algebraic solution exists.

The computational complexity of checking that sufficiently many pp-curvatures vanish is O~​(Δb6​B)=O~​(H12​n−6​n12​n​3−3​n)\tilde{O}(\Delta_{b}^{6}B)=\tilde{O}(H^{12n-6}n^{12n}3^{-3n}) where the notation O~\tilde{O} hides factors that are polynomial in nn and logarithmic in HH.

We also explain how the problem of deciding algebraicity of solutions of first-order differential equations with algebraic coefficients reduces to the case of rational coefficients as in the theorem above.

Moreover, we treat algorithmic aspects of the result and report on an implementation. We rely on a fast algorithm by Bostan and Schost [9] to quickly compute pp-curvatures of first-order equations. The algorithm presented in this text does not outperform other known algorithms for certifying that a first-order differential equation has algebraic solutions, however in generic cases the algorithm detects quickly the presence of a transcendental solution, especially when the degree and size of the coefficients explode. We expect that any significant improvement in our approach for certifying the algebraicity of solutions would come from new theoretical results rather than algorithmic optimization. Although theoretically the algorithm could treat the case of differential equations with algebraic non-rational coefficients, we did not optimize it to treat this case efficiently.

Our algorithm provides an instance of deciding algebraicity of D-finite functions using exclusively an arithmetic criterion. One could hope for results, similar in spirit, for first-order differential equations with algebraic coefficients, and for higher order equations in which the pp-curvature conjecture is proven. The computation of pp-curvatures for arbitrary order differential equations and deciding their nullity is possible and algorithms exist to perform these computations efficiently [5, 6].

Proving transcendence of solutions using our algorithm does not rely on our main results, Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, while proving algebraicity using these theorems is highly inefficient. Thus we stress that the theoretical results of this paper, in particular the effective version of Kronecker’s Theorem, should be seen as its main contribution.

Structure of the Paper.

In Section 2 we revisit Honda’s proof of the pp-curvature conjecture for first-order differential equations by investigating its equivalence with Kronecker’s Theorem in view of effective aspects. Relying on Theorem 1.2, we give a proof of Theorem 1.3, with the exception of the stated computational complexity. In Section 3 we discuss different effective approaches to the pp-curvature conjecture for first-order equations. The proof of Theorem 1.2 takes up the entirety of Section 4, in which we adapt the Chudnovskys’ proof of Kronecker’s Theorem. Afterwards, in Section 5, we describe an algorithm that decides the algebraicity of the solution of first-order differential equation using the computation of pp-curvatures. Its complexity estimate, worked out in Proposition 5.17 finishes the proof of Theorem 1.3. Finally, in the last section, Section 6, we discuss our implementation of this algorithm in SageMath.

2 Reformulations of the Problem

This section contains no new results. Its purpose is to describe the equivalence between the pp-curvature conjecture for the first-order equation (2) and Kronecker’s Theorem 1.1. The results can be found in one form or another in the literature [18, 11, 51, 4].

We consider the equation (2) with u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x). A nonzero solution y⁡(x)y(x) has the form y⁡(x)=exp⁡(∫u⁡(x)​𝑑x)y(x)=\exp(\int u(x)\mathrm{d}x). This expression combines two operations that do not preserve rationality or algebraicity in different ways. A primitive of a rational function remains a rational function if and only if all its residues are zero, whereas a fraction αx−β\frac{\alpha}{x-\beta} has a logarithm as its primitive. Contrarily, the exponential acts in such a way that for a nonzero algebraic function f⁡(x)f(x), the function exp⁡(f⁡(x))\exp(f(x)) is transcendental. This can be seen as a particular case of a conjecture by Schanuel about the transcendence degree of a set of power series and their exponentials, that was proven by Ax [2].

Hence, for a function y⁡(x)=exp⁡(∫u⁡(x)​𝑑x)y(x)=\exp(\int u(x)\mathrm{d}x) to be algebraic, u⁡(x)u(x) cannot have a polynomial part or poles of order more than one, so that y⁡(x)y(x) factors into a product of (x−β)α(x-\beta)^{\alpha} where β\beta is a pole of u⁡(x)u(x), and α\alpha is the residue at β\beta. For such u⁡(x)u(x), the function y⁡(x)y(x) is algebraic if and only if the residues of u⁡(x)u(x) are rational numbers.

Remark 2.1.

We used the fact that the function xαx^{\alpha} is algebraic if and only if α\alpha is rational. Indeed, if α\alpha is rational, clearly xαx^{\alpha} is algebraic. Assume conversely, that xαx^{\alpha} is algebraic. Then there exists a non-zero relation of the form ∑m,ncm,n​xα​m+n=0\sum_{m,n}c_{m,n}x^{\alpha m+n}=0. In particular, as the functions xβx^{\beta} for β∈ℂ\beta\in\mathbb{C} are ℂ\mathbb{C}-linearly independent, there have to exist m1,m2,n1,n2∈ℕm_{1},m_{2},n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{N}, such that xα​m1+n1=xα​m2+n2x^{\alpha m_{1}+n_{1}}=x^{\alpha m_{2}+n_{2}}, i.e., α=(n2−n1)/(m1−m2)\alpha=(n_{2}-n_{1})/(m_{1}-m_{2}) is rational.

A convenient way to compute the residues of the rational function u⁡(x)u(x) is provided by Rothstein-Trager resultant [42, 43, 48]. We state their result here in a simplified, but for our purposes sufficient, form.

Theorem 2.2 (Rothstein, Trager).

Let u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x) be a rational function with only simple poles and deg⁡a⁡(x)<deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<\deg b(x). Then its residues are precisely the roots of the Rothstein-Trager resultant

R⁡(w)≔resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x)).R(w)\coloneqq\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)).

We investigate complexity estimates for the Rothstein-Trager resultant in Section 5.1. Altogether we get the following equivalent characterizations.

Proposition 2.3.

The following statements for the differential equation (2) are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    All solutions of (2) are algebraic.

  2. (2)

    The coefficient u⁡(x)u(x) can be written as

    u⁡(x)=∑i=1nαix−βiu(x)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{x-\beta_{i}} (3)

    with distinct algebraic poles βi∈ℚ¯\beta_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and rational residues αi∈ℚ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}.

  3. (3)

    We have deg⁡a⁡(x)<deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<\deg b(x), all poles of u⁡(x)u(x) are simple and its Rothstein-Trager resultant factors into linear factors in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w].

The conditions on the degree and the poles of u⁡(x)u(x) in the third item are equivalent to the differential equation (2) being Fuchsian.

Similar considerations hold in characteristic pp. Moreover, by Cartier’s Lemma, the existence of a non-zero solution of a first-order differential equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) is equivalent to the vanishing of its pp-curvature22 2 The existence of a non-zero polynomial solution in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], a non-zero algebraic solution in 𝔽p​[[x]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![x]\!] or any non-zero solution in 𝔽p​[[x]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![x]\!] are equivalent [18, Lem. 1].. In the particular case of first-order equations, the pp-curvature is given by a one-dimensional matrix, whose entry we also call, by abuse of notation, the pp-curvature. There is an explicit formula for this pp-curvature in terms of the coefficient u⁡(x)u(x), that already implicitly appears in Jacobson’s work [19]: it is given by u​(x)p+u(p−1)​(x)u(x)^{p}+u^{(p-1)}(x).

Putting all these observations together, we infer the following results characterizing the existence of (algebraic) solutions in characteristic pp.

Proposition 2.4.

Let pp be a prime number. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    The pp-curvature u​(x)p+u(p−1)​(x)u(x)^{p}+u^{(p-1)}(x) of (2) vanishes.

  2. (2)

    The reduction of (2) has an algebraic solution in 𝔽p​[[x]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![x]\!].

  3. (3)

    The coefficient u⁡(x)u(x) can be written as

    u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)b⁡(x)=∑i=1nαix−βi,u(x)=\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{x-\beta_{i}},

    with βi∈𝔽¯p\beta_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p} and αi∈𝔽p\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}.

  4. (4)

    We have deg⁡a⁡(x)<deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<\deg b(x), all poles of u⁡(x)u(x) are simple and its Rothstein-Trager resultant factors into linear factors in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w].

The equivalence of (1) and (2) is Cartier’s Lemma (see [4, Theorem 3.19] for a precise statement and proof). Statements (3) and (4) are equivalent by Theorem 2.2. Assuming (3) we can write down an explicit algebraic solution, hence (3) implies (2). Finally, by Jacobson’s formula, the vanishing of the pp-curvature of Equation (2) implies that the partial fraction decomposition of u⁡(x)u(x) has precisely the shape given in (3).

Honda’s proof of the pp-curvature conjecture for (2) essentially consists in recognizing that Kronecker’s Theorem implies that if (4) in Proposition 2.4 holds for almost all prime numbers pp, then (3) in Proposition 2.3 holds as well. Our following considerations throughout this article are focused on the question, whether (4) in Proposition 2.4 for finitely many prime numbers suffices to conclude (3) in Proposition 2.3.

Note that Honda actually proved more, namely that the pp-curvature conjecture for first-order equations is equivalent to Kronecker’s Theorem. We refer the reader for the other implication to Honda’s original article [18].

Let us next investigate which prime numbers are exceptional in the sense that there is no solution of the reduction of the differential equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) with u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x) in 𝔽p​[[x]],\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![x]\!], despite the existence of a solution in characteristic 00. In other words we are investigating for which prime numbers assertion (4) in Proposition 2.4 might be false, although (3) in Proposition 2.3 holds. Trivially, if a polynomial splits in ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x] into linear factors, it splits into linear factors in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] not just for almost all prime numbers, but for all prime numbers. However, it might happen that the degree of b⁡(x)b(x) drops, when reduced modulo pp, or that two distinct poles of u⁡(x)u(x) of order 11 collapse to a pole of higher order, when reduced modulo pp. Luckily, both of these exceptions can be easily read off the leading coefficient (up to sign) Δb=|res⁡(b⁡(x),−b′​(x))|\Delta_{b}=|\res(b(x),-b^{\prime}(x))| of the Rothstein-Trager resultant, as already noticed by van der Put, c.f. [51, Prop. 3.2(2)].

Proposition 2.5.

Assume that y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) with u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x) has an algebraic solution. If p​|Δbp\not\hskip 2.5pt\mid\Delta_{b} then the pp-curvature of the equation vanishes.

The following example illustrates both types of exceptional primes.

Example 2.6.

Consider the rational function

u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)b⁡(x)=x+22​x2+x−1=56⋅1x−12−13⋅1x+1u(x)=\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}=\frac{x+2}{2x^{2}+x-1}=\frac{5}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{x-\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{x+1}

and the associated differential equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x). It has the algebraic solution y⁡(x)=(2​x−1)5/6(x+1)1/3y(x)=\frac{\left(2x-1\right)^{{5}/{6}}}{\left(x+1\right)^{{1}/{3}}}, which cannot be reduced modulo 22 and 33, but modulo all other prime numbers. The resultant res⁡(b⁡(x),−b′​(x))\res(b(x),-b^{\prime}(x)) is equal to −18-18. For p=2p=2 the denominator of u⁡(x)u(x) reduces to a degree one polynomial. For p=3p=3 the two poles x=12x=\frac{1}{2} and x=−1x=-1 collapse to a single pole of order 22.

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.3, assuming Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

First, we can reduce without loss of generality to the case c=1c=1. Indeed, if y⁡(x)y(x) satisfies y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x), then (y​(x)c)′=c⋅u⁡(x)​y​(x)c(y(x)^{c})^{\prime}=c\cdot u(x)y(x)^{c} and for a given c∈ℚc\in\mathbb{Q}, the function y⁡(x)y(x) is algebraic if and only if y​(x)cy(x)^{c} is algebraic.

By Theorem 1.2, R⁡(w)R(w) factors into linear factors in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w] if and only if its reduction also splits completely in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w] for all prime numbers pp up to σ\sigma, not dividing Δb\Delta_{b}. Note that Δb\Delta_{b} is non-zero by the assumption that b⁡(x)b(x) is square-free. By Proposition 2.4, using that deg⁡a⁡(x)<deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<\deg b(x), this in turn is equivalent to the vanishing of the pp-curvatures for all prime numbers not dividing Δb\Delta_{b} and smaller than σ\sigma.

The complexity estimates follow from Proposition 5.17. ∎

Remark 2.7.

By Proposition 2.3, the equation having a non-zero algebraic solution is equivalent to deg⁡b⁡(x)>deg⁡a⁡(x)\deg b(x)>\deg a(x), that b⁡(x)b(x) only has simple poles, and that R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x)CLOSER(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x) factors in linear factors in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w]. We check here the first two conditions directly. However, if one of them is not met, it is also not met when reducing u⁡(x)u(x) modulo almost all primes, so by Proposition 2.4 almost all pp-curvatures will not vanish. Having said that, the bound on the primes in this case is not controlled solely by the Rothstein-Trager resultant, as the following example illustrates: Let a⁡(x)=A​x+1,b⁡(x)=xa(x)=Ax+1,b(x)=x for A∈ℚA\in\mathbb{Q}. Then the Rothstein-Trager resultant is R⁡(w)=−w+1R(w)=-w+1 for every choice of AA. Assume we use Theorem 1.2 to obtain a bound σ\sigma on the numbers of pp-curvatures to check to decide algebraicity. If we now set A=σ!A=\sigma!, the pp-curvatures of our differential equation will vanish up to σ\sigma, but will not vanish for any prime larger than σ\sigma.

Finally we note that our arguments can easily be extended to equations y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) with u​(x)∈ℚ¯​[x]u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[x] by using the following well-known result, that is a direct consequence of Vieta’s formulas.

Proposition 2.8.

Let KK be a number field, let R⁡(w)∈K⁡[w]R(w)\in K[w] with leading coefficient rn∈K\{0}r_{n}\in K\backslash\{0\}. If R⁡(w)R(w) splits completely over KK with all its roots in ℚ\mathbb{Q}, then 1rn​R​(w)\frac{1}{r_{n}}R(w) is a polynomial in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w].

3 Other Approaches

3.1 Finding Rational Roots

Once we have computed the Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)∈ℚ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Q}[w] associated to u⁡(x)u(x), checking the rationality of the residues (and thus solving the problem of deciding algebraicity of the solutions of (2)) amounts to finding the rational roots of R⁡(w)R(w). Then the residues of the rational function u⁡(x)u(x) are all rational if and only if its Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)R(w) splits completely over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

A naïve approach to finding the rational roots of a polynomial is to factor it completely over ℚ\mathbb{Q} and consider the factors of degree one. However this is more than what we are looking for and specific more efficient algorithms to find the rational roots of a polynomial exist. We refer the reader to [13, §14-16] and [7, §21] for details about such algorithms and an analysis of their complexity.

We obtain Algorithm 1.

Remark 3.1.

Starting from a rational function in u​(x)∈ℚ¯​[x]u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[x], deciding the algebraicity of solutions of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) reduces to the same problem. Following Proposition 2.8, once we have computed the Rothstein-Trager resultant, we can divide by its leading coefficient and if the obtained polynomial has non-rational coefficients we can conclude on the transcendence of the solutions of the input differential equation. Else we continue with the polynomial in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w] as described in this section.

3.2 The Least Prime That Does Not Split in a Number Field

The matter of bounding the least rational prime number that does not split completely in a given (Galois) number field has been extensively studied in the literature. It is a special case of the more general problem of finding an upper bound on the least prime that has a prescribed splitting pattern in a number field [26, 1, 22], in accordance with the Chebotarev Density Theorem. More precisely, given a Galois field extension K/ℚK/\mathbb{Q} of degree dd and discriminant DD, there are several asymptotic estimates on the size of the smallest rational prime that does not split completely in KK. An explicit statement was proven by Vaaler and Voloch [50, Thm. 1].

Theorem 3.2 (Vaaler, Voloch).

Let K/ℚK/\mathbb{Q} be a number field of degree dd and discriminant DD. If exp⁡(max⁡{105,25​(log⁡(d))2})≤8​D12​(d−1)\exp(\max\{105,25(\log(d))^{2}\})\leq 8D^{\frac{1}{2(d-1)}} then there exists a prime pp, such that pp does not split completely in KK and p≤26​d2​D12​(d−1)p\leq 26d^{2}D^{\frac{1}{2(d-1)}}.

Sharper, asymptotic bounds were proven, both under the assumption of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis by Murty [32], and unconditionally [32, 27].

For a prime pp splitting completely in the splitting field of a polynomial R⁡(w)R(w) is equivalent to the reduction of R⁡(w)R(w) modulo pp splitting into linear factors in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w], except for finitely many primes.

If L/ℚL/\mathbb{Q} is the splitting field of R⁡(w)∈ℚ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Q}[w], then R⁡(w)R(w) splits completely in LL, and it splits completely in any of the residue fields of LL. Let pp be a prime of ℤ\mathbb{Z} that splits completely in LL, then in particular the corresponding residue fields of LL are equal to their prime fields 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} [33, §1, Prop. 8.2, p. 46; p. 49], so R⁡(w)R(w) splits completely over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

The other implication can be shown by applying the Dedekind-Kummer Theorem [33, §1, Prop. 8.3]: We can reduce to the case where R⁡(w)R(w) is monic and in ℤ⁡[w]\mathbb{Z}[w] (divide by its leading coefficient and consider mdeg⁡(R)​R​(w/m)m^{\deg(R)}R(w/m) for m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z} a common denominator of its coefficients). Consider an irreducible factor of R⁡(w)R(w) of degree at least 22 with root α\alpha. This factor will split completely modulo pp for almost all primes of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Hence in K1=K⁡(α)K_{1}=K(\alpha) the Dedekind-Kummer Theorem states that almost all primes of ℤ\mathbb{Z} split completely. We then repeat the argument with the root of an irreducible factor of R⁡(w)R(w) of degree at least 22 over K1K_{1} and so on until reaching Kr=LK_{r}=L. Each step excludes finitely many primes, thus almost all primes split completely in LL.

This gives another approach to finding an effective version of Kronecker’s Theorem. There seem to exist obstacles, however.

First, most results in this direction are of asymptotic nature, making it hard to convert them into an explicit bound. The exception is Vaaler and Voloch’s statement given above. However, they have an assumption on the minimal size of DD that exceeds the computational capacity of modern computers. Li claims [27, p. 1062] that this assumption is artificial and better results could be expected for small DD.

Second, one would need to estimate, given a polynomial R⁡(w)R(w), the discriminant and the degree of a potential splitting field of R⁡(w)R(w). Given that we cannot assume R⁡(w)R(w) to be irreducible, the discriminant of the polynomial and the discriminant of its splitting field are not related in an obvious way.

While both of these problems seem to be manageable in principle, we are not aware of any algorithm for solving our problem based on this approach.

3.3 Indicial Equations

As discussed in Section 2, the problem of deciding algebraicity of the solutions of (2) can be solved by investigating its singularities, and, in particular by deciding whether the residues of the rational function coefficient u⁡(x)u(x) are rational. Working directly in the framework of differential equations instead, we have the following addition to Proposition 2.3.

Proposition 3.3.

The following statements for the differential equation (2) are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    All solutions of (2) are algebraic.

  2. (4)

    All singularities of (2) are regular singular and its local exponent at each of these singularities is rational.

Proof.

The singularities of (2) are precisely the poles of u⁡(x)u(x), and possibly ∞\infty. As the order of the differential equation is 11, a singularity at x0x_{0} is regular, if and only if the valuation of u⁡(x)u(x) at x0x_{0} is at least −1-1, i.e., if the pole of u⁡(x)u(x) is of order at most 11. The local exponent at x0x_{0} is precisely given by the residue of u⁡(x)u(x) at x0x_{0}. Investigating the singularity at ∞\infty amounts to investigate the behavior of −x2​y′​(x)=u⁡(1x)​y​(x)-x^{2}y^{\prime}(x)=u(\frac{1}{x})y(x) at 00. So the singularity is present, if and only if deg⁡a⁡(x)≥deg⁡b⁡(x)−1\deg a(x)\geq\deg b(x)-1 and it is regular if and only if deg⁡a⁡(x)=deg⁡b⁡(x)−1\deg a(x)=\deg b(x)-1. The local exponent at ∞\infty automatically is rational if u⁡(x)u(x) has rational coefficients. So we have shown that (4) is equivalent to assertion (2) of Proposition 2.3. ∎

To use this equivalent criterion to decide algebraicity of solutions, one can factor b⁡(x)b(x) to determine the singularities of the equation and then compute the local exponents by computing the indicial polynomial at the zeroes of b⁡(x)b(x). This polynomial is of degree one with coefficients in the splitting field of b⁡(x)b(x). Its root is rational, if and only if it is a ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-multiple of a polynomial in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x].

This approach leads to the following algorithm.

4 An Effective Version of Kronecker’s Theorem

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.2. We outline the steps here. In [11] D.V. and G.V. Chudnovsky provide an elementary proof of Kronecker’s Theorem (and with it, according to the discussion in Section 2, of Honda’s proof of the pp-curvature conjecture for first-order equations) using Hermite-Padé approximation.

One main ingredient is the fact that the function xαx^{\alpha}, for example defined, setting z≔x−1z\coloneqq x-1, by the power series

xα=∑n≥0(αn)​(x−1)n=∑n≥0(αn)​zn,x^{\alpha}=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}\binom{\alpha}{n}(x-1)^{n}=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}\binom{\alpha}{n}z^{n},

is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x) if and only if α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, see Remark 2.1. We will assume by contradiction that a root α\alpha is irrational, although its annihilating polynomial for almost all prime numbers pp splits into linear factors.

The next ingredient is Hermite-Padé approximation. The ideas of this method were first introduced by Hermite in [16] to prove the transcendence of ee, and then extended by him and Padé, his student [17, 34, 35]. It produces for a finite number of power series, a list of polynomials of prescribed degrees, such that the sum of the power series, weighted by the polynomials, has highest possible order. More precisely, let KK be a field. Let f1​(z),…,fm​(z)∈K⁡[[z]]f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{m}(z)\in K[\![z]\!] be a tuple of power series. Let n1,…,nmn_{1},\ldots,n_{m} be non-negative integers and let P1​(z),…,Pm​(z)∈K⁡[z]P_{1}(z),\ldots,P_{m}(z)\in K[z] be polynomials of degree n1,…,nmn_{1},\ldots,n_{m} respectively. If the power series

g⁡(z)≔P1​(z)​f1​(z)+⋯+Pm​(z)​fm​(z)∈K⁡[[z]]g(z)\coloneqq P_{1}(z)f_{1}(z)+\cdots+P_{m}(z)f_{m}(z)\in K[\![z]\!]

has order greater than or equal to n1+⋯+nm+m−1n_{1}+\cdots+n_{m}+m-1 at 00, then the tuple (P1​(z),…,Pm​(z))(P_{1}(z),\ldots,P_{m}(z)) is called a Hermite-Padé approximant to (f1​(z),…,fm​(z))(f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{m}(z)) of type (n1,…,nm)(n_{1},\ldots,n_{m}), and g⁡(z)g(z) is called the remainder of the approximation. For further exposition of the concept, see [29, 21, 20].

In the following, a well-known formula for some Hermite-Padé approximants of the consecutive powers (1−z)(i−1)​α(1-z)^{(i-1)\alpha} with α∉ℚ\alpha\not\in\mathbb{Q} for 1≤i≤2​M+11\leq i\leq 2M+1, with coefficients of uniform degree NN for any integer values of MM and NN is exploited. It was introduced by Padé in [36] and studied and extended by Jager, Mahler, and G. Chudnovsky [20, 29, 12], but could already be deduced from Hermite’s work [16]. The result also includes an explicit expression for the first non-vanishing term in this approximation.

It is clear that this first non-vanishing term of this approximation will be an algebraic number. In the following one considers a certain multiple of this coefficient. One can estimate its norm, and its denominator by two different estimates, coming from either side of the equation for the Hermite-Padé approximation, depending on MM and NN. The bound on the denominator uses the fact that if α\alpha reduces to an integer modulo a prime pp, certain binomial coefficients involving α\alpha have non-negative pp-adic valuation. From there, Chudnovsky and Chudnovsky use an asymptotic argument, that for sufficiently large MM and NN, the bounds contradict the trivial inequality that the norm of a non-zero algebraic integer is greater or equal to one.

We will argue along the same lines, but we will not work asymptotically, but find upper bounds on the values of MM and NN for the contradiction to occur. In addition, we use that the argument of the Chudnovsky brothers relies on ruling out prime divisors of the denominators of a finite set of binomial coefficients, in whose denominators a priori only prime factors to a bound σ\sigma depending on MM and NN may appear. This allows us to conclude if we assume that R⁡(w)R(w) factors into linear factors modulo pp for all primes pp up to σ\sigma.

For the rest of the section we fix an irrational number α\alpha with square-free annihilating polynomial R⁡(w)=rn​wn+⋯+r1​w+r0R(w)=r_{n}w^{n}+\cdots+r_{1}w+r_{0} with rn>0r_{n}>0. We set ΔR≔resw⁡(R⁡(w),R′​(w))≠0\Delta_{R}\coloneq\res_{w}(R(w),R^{\prime}(w))\neq 0, we define δ⁡(ΔR)≔∏p|ΔRp1/(p−1),\delta(\Delta_{R})\coloneqq\prod_{p|\Delta_{R}}p^{1/(p-1)}, and we pick B∈ℝB\in\mathbb{R} to be a bound on the maximal modulus of a root of R⁡(w)R(w). We let LL be the splitting field of RR. The denominator den⁡(γ)\den(\gamma) of γ∈L\gamma\in L is the smallest positive integer a∈ℕ>0a\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}, such that a​γ∈𝒪La\gamma\in\mathcal{O}_{L}, the ring of integers of LL. In particular, we have den⁡(α)|rn\den(\alpha)|r_{n}. Let M,NM,N be two positive integers and define σ=σ⁡(M,N)≔(2​M+1)​N+2​M\sigma=\sigma(M,N)\coloneqq(2M+1)N+2M. We will assume that R⁡(w)R(w) splits into linear factors for all primes up to σ\sigma, that do not divide rnr_{n}. The proof of Theorem 1.2 is equivalent to showing that when choosing M≔⌈2.826⋅rn3⋅δ⁡(ΔR)⌉M\coloneqq\left\lceil 2.826\cdot r_{n}^{3}\cdot\delta(\Delta_{R})\right\rceil and N≔6.076⋅B​MN\coloneqq 6.076\cdot BM the above assumptions lead to a contradiction. We will accomplish this in Proposition 4.12, contradicting Corollary 4.10.

4.1.1 Bounding the Denominator

The following lemma is the key ingredient in the proof of Proposition 4.2, and as such, also the key ingredient to reducing Kronecker’s Theorem to a statement about a finite number of primes. We denote by vp​(⋅)v_{p}(\cdot) the pp-adic valuation.

Lemma 4.4.

Let k,s∈ℤk,s\in\mathbb{Z}, t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, and let pp be a prime number. Let α\alpha be given as the zero of a square-free polynomial R⁡(w)∈ℤ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Z}[w] with leading coefficient rnr_{n} and ΔR≔resw⁡(R⁡(w),R′​(w))\Delta_{R}\coloneqq\res_{w}(R(w),R^{\prime}(w)).

    If p​|ΔRp\not\hskip 2.5pt\mid\Delta_{R} and R⁡(w)modpR(w)\bmod p splits completely in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w], then p​|den⁡((k​α+st))p\not\hskip 2.5pt\mid\den\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right).

  2.  (2)

    If p​|rnp\not\hskip 2.5pt\mid r_{n} and p|den⁡((k​α+st))p|\den\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right), then p≤tp\leq t and vp​((k​α+st))≥−⌊tp−1⌋v_{p}\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right)\geq-\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p-1}\right\rfloor.

  3.  (3)

    If vp​(rn)=vv_{p}(r_{n})=v, then vp​((k​α+st))≥−(v​t+⌊tp−1⌋)v_{p}\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right)\geq-\left(vt+\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p-1}\right\rfloor\right).

    If R⁡(w)modpR(w)\bmod p splits completely in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w] for all primes p≤tp\leq t not dividing rnr_{n}, then den⁡((k​α+st))\den\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right) divides rnt​∏p|ΔRp⌊tp−1⌋.r_{n}^{t}\prod_{p\mid\Delta_{R}}p^{\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p-1}\right\rfloor}.

Proof.

If R⁡(w)modpR(w)\bmod p splits in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w], and p​|ΔRp\not\hskip 2.5pt\mid\Delta_{R} then all of its zeroes are distinct elements of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. Then, by Hensel’s Lemma [33, (4.6) p.129] R⁡(w)R(w) splits over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} into linear factors, i.e. α∈ℤp\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. It follows that (k​α+st)∈ℚp\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\in\mathbb{Q}_{p} and we want to show that vp​((k​α+st))≥0v_{p}\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right)\geq 0. For all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} there exists aj∈ℤa_{j}\in\mathbb{Z} such that α=aj+cj​pj\alpha=a_{j}+c_{j}p^{j} where cj∈ℤpc_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. It follows that (k​α+st)=(k​aj+st)+bj​pjt!\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}=\binom{ka_{j}+s}{t}+b_{j}\frac{p^{j}}{t!} for some bj∈ℤpb_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. Now vp​((k​α+st))≥min⁡(vp​((k​aj+st)),vp​(bj​pjt!))v_{p}\left(\binom{k\alpha+s}{t}\right)\geq\min\left(v_{p}\left(\binom{ka_{j}+s}{t}\right),v_{p}\left(b_{j}\frac{p^{j}}{t!}\right)\right). Since aj∈ℤa_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}, (k​aj+st)∈ℤ\binom{ka_{j}+s}{t}\in\mathbb{Z} and its pp-adic valuation is non-negative for all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}. 4.2 A Bound on the Number of Primes

Finally, combining the results of Propositions 4.2 and 4.7 we get an upper bound on the integer |den⁡(Ω​gσ)d​NormL/ℚ⁡(Ω​gσ)||\den(\Omega g_{\sigma})^{d}\Norm_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\Omega g_{\sigma})|. To prepare for further estimates, we split it into three parts and set

X⁡(M)≔C02​M−1​rn6​M+1​δ6​M+1(2​M+1)2​M+1=1C02​rn2​δ2⋅(C0​rn3​δ32​M+1)2​M+1Y⁡(M,N)≔exp⁡(π​B​u1​(M)+4​log⁡(43)​B2​u2​(M)N)⋅(2​M+1)−2​M−1/2⋅(2​e2​rn5​δ2π2)MZ⁡(M,N)≔(1N)M⋅exp⁡(M+16​N).\begin{array}[]{cl}X(M)&\coloneqq\cfrac{C_{0}^{2M-1}r_{n}^{6M+1}\delta^{6M+1}}{(2M+1)^{2M+1}}=\cfrac{1}{C_{0}^{2}r_{n}^{2}\delta^{2}}\cdot\left(\cfrac{C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3}}{2M+1}\right)^{2M+1}\\ Y(M,N)&\coloneqq\exp\left(\pi Bu_{1}(M)+4\log\left(\cfrac{4}{3}\right)B^{2}\cfrac{u_{2}(M)}{N}\right)\cdot(2M+1)^{-2M-1/2}\cdot\left(\cfrac{2e^{2}r_{n}^{5}\delta^{2}}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{M}\\ Z(M,N)&\coloneqq\left(\cfrac{1}{N}\right)^{M}\cdot\exp\left(\cfrac{M+1}{6N}\right).\end{array}

The factor X⁡(M)X(M) consists of factors from the upper bound of Propositions 4.2 and 4.7 that are raised to the power NN. In this sense, it is the main contribution of the upper bound as NN grows. The factor Y⁡(M,N)Y(M,N) consists of non-negligible factors with respect to MM, its behavior as MM grows will determine how large we need NN to be with respect to MM for our bound to become smaller than 11. Finally, in Z⁡(M,N)Z(M,N) we group factors that are negligible for the growth behavior of the bound.

Of course, these quantities also depend on rnr_{n}, and ΔR\Delta_{R}, which are suppressed in the notation. Moreover, once we fix MM to be a function of rn,ΔRr_{n},\Delta_{R}, the notation becomes particularly misleading. However, in the following calculations it will be convenient to view these quantities as functions of MM and NN.

Corollary 4.10.

Let M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N} and N≥4​M​B.N\geq 4MB. Then

0<|den⁡(Ω​gσ)​NormL/ℚ​(Ω​gσ)1d|<X​(M)N⋅Y⁡(M,N)⋅Z⁡(M,N).0<|\den(\Omega g_{\sigma})\Norm_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\Omega g_{\sigma})^{\frac{1}{d}}|<X(M)^{N}\cdot Y(M,N)\cdot Z(M,N). (14)

From the asymptotics of these bounds, one can easily deduce the existence of parameters MM and NN, such that |den⁡(Ω​gσ)​NormL/ℚ​(Ω​gσ)1d|<1|\den(\Omega g_{\sigma})\Norm_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\Omega g_{\sigma})^{\frac{1}{d}}|<1. For large enough MM compared to rn,ΔRr_{n},\Delta_{R}, the expression X⁡(M)X(M) is strictly smaller than 11. Moreover, if we choose NN large enough with respect to MM, we have X​(M)N<Y​(M,N)−1X(M)^{N}<Y(M,N)^{-1}, as the right-hand side is increasing with NN. Finally, for N>M>3N>M>3, clearly Z⁡(M,N)<1Z(M,N)<1. Thus, for this choice of M,NM,N we find the desired contradiction to the assumption that α\alpha was irrational, and so we have proved Kronecker’s Theorem. This argumentation was carried out by the Chudnovsky brothers in [11]. The rest of this subsection is devoted to showing that our explicit choices of MM and NN suffice for the contradiction to occur.

4.2.1 Choice of the Number of Functions to Approximate

Let us first justify our choice of MM.

Lemma 4.11.

For any M>12​(C0​rn3​δ3−1)M>\frac{1}{2}(C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3}-1) we have X⁡(M)<1X(M)<1. Moreover, for M>C0​rn3​δ3M>C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3} we have X⁡(M)<2−(2​M+1)​(C0​rn​δ)−2X(M)<2^{-(2M+1)}(C_{0}r_{n}\delta)^{-2}.

Proof.

The proof consists of a straightforward computation. ∎

The choices of MM and NN are dependent on each other in the following way: the function X⁡(M)X(M) is decreasing with MM, while simultaneously Y⁡(M,N)Y(M,N) increases. Thus, the first value of NN, such that X​(M)N​Y​(M,N)​Z​(M,N)<1X(M)^{N}Y(M,N)Z(M,N)<1 varies in a non-obvious way with MM. To obtain tight bounds one should minimize σ=(2​M+1)​N+2​M\sigma=(2M+1)N+2M under the constraint X​(M)N​Y​(M,N)​Z​(M,N)<1X(M)^{N}Y(M,N)Z(M,N)<1. We carry out no such computations, but are content with M=⌈C0​rn3​δ3⌉M=\lceil C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3}\rceil. Naïve estimates and computations suggest that picking M≈⌈0.806⋅C0​rn3​δ3⌉M\approx\lceil 0.806\cdot C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3}\rceil yields slightly more optimal values for σ\sigma.

The goal of this section is to prove that for the explicit values of MM and NN given in Theorem 1.2 the right-hand side of (14) is bounded from above by 11. We assume M=⌈C0​rn3​δ3⌉M=\lceil C_{0}r_{n}^{3}\delta^{3}\rceil to be fixed. In Proposition 4.7, we assume NN to depend at least linearly on BB and MM. Let us set N≔A​B​MN\coloneqq ABM for some constant A≥4A\geq 4 to be determined later. With these choices of MM and NN the right-hand side of (14) is a function in rnr_{n} and ΔR\Delta_{R}. 5 Algorithm and Complexity

The bounds we present in Theorem 1.3 allow us, as was our purpose, to solve algorithmically the problem of deciding the algebraicity of solutions of equations (2). We present here an algorithm, Algorithm 3, solving this problem and we estimate its complexity. Each of its steps is studied in what follows, and the full algorithm’s complexity estimate is analyzed in Section 5.5. It turns out to be inefficient, compared to other, more straight-forward, approaches for certifying algebraicity, cf. Corollary 5.11. All complexities are stated in number of bit operations.

Throughout this section, we consider our input rational function u⁡(x)u(x) to be of normal form a⁡(x)b⁡(x)\frac{a(x)}{b(x)} where a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x) have integer coefficients, are primitive, coprime, and deg⁡a⁡(x)<deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<\deg b(x). The primitivity condition can be made without loss of generality, as already discussed in the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Section 2. This comes from the fact that if y⁡(x)y(x) satisfies y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x), then for any c∈ℚc\in\mathbb{Q}, the function y~​(x)≔y​(x)c\tilde{y}(x)\coloneqq y(x)^{c} satisfies y~′​(x)=c⋅u⁡(x)​y~​(x)\tilde{y}^{\prime}(x)=c\cdot u(x)\tilde{y}(x), and y⁡(x)y(x) is algebraic if and only if y~​(x)\tilde{y}(x) is algebraic.

Our measure of complexity of a rational number will be an estimate of ‘‘its size on a computer’’, that we call its height. More precisely, if q=a/b∈ℚq=a/b\in\mathbb{Q} with a,b∈ℤ∖{0}a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\} coprime, the height of qq is h⁡(q)≔log2⁡(|a​b|)h(q)\coloneqq\log_{2}(|ab|), and we set the height of 00 to be 11. The height h⁡(f⁡(x))h(f(x)) of f⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x] is the maximum of the heights of its coefficients, and its multiplicative height is H⁡(f⁡(x))≔2h⁡(f⁡(x))H(f(x))\coloneqq 2^{h(f(x))}. Remark that if f⁡(x)f(x) has integer coefficients, then H⁡(f⁡(x))H(f(x)) is the maximum of the modulus of its coefficients. The height of a rational function u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x) with a⁡(x),b⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]a(x),b(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] primitive and coprime, is the maximum of h⁡(a⁡(x))h(a(x)) and h⁡(b⁡(x))h(b(x)).

The computation of the normal form, as described above, of u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x) of height hh and degree n−1n-1 in the numerator and nn in the denominator requires computing the greatest common divisor of n+1n+1 numbers and the greatest common divisor of two polynomials. The computation of the greatest common divisor of two polynomials in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x] of degree at most nn and height hh can be made by performing O~​(n​h)\tilde{O}(nh) bit operations [13, Corollary 11.9, p.325]. With an adaptation of the same algorithm we can compute the gcd of two integers of height at most hh in O~​(h)\tilde{O}(h) bit operations. Hence applying it nn times allows to compute the greatest common divisor of n+1n+1 integers of height at most hh in O~​(n​h)\tilde{O}(nh) bit operations, thus computing the normal form of u⁡(x)u(x) can be made by performing O~​(n​h)\tilde{O}(nh) bit operations.

Additionally, we will assume in the following that the Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) is square-free to lighten the exposition. If it is not, we replace it with its square-free part, which can be readily computed as R⁡(w)/gcd⁡(R⁡(w),R′​(w))R(w)/\gcd(R(w),R^{\prime}(w)) in negligible bit operation cost. The polynomial R⁡(w)R(w) and its square-free part have the same roots, hence the same bound BB on their modulus, and the same prime factors of the leading coefficient. However, the height of R⁡(w)R(w) might be altered when taking the square-free part. We prove an estimate in Proposition 5.7 that ensures the order of the height remains the same.

Last, to avoid costly integer factoring of the potentially large resultant ΔR\Delta_{R} to compute δ\delta, we prove an estimate in Proposition 5.15.

Remark 5.1.

As explained in Remark 3.1, starting from u​(x)∈ℚ¯​(x)u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x), we can check if R~​(w)≔R⁡(w)/Δb\tilde{R}(w)\coloneqq R(w)/\Delta_{b} is in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w] after step 4. If this is not the case we can immediately conclude that the output has to be Transcendental with Proposition 2.8. Otherwise, we can continue from step 5 after replacement of R⁡(w)R(w) by the polynomial in ℤ⁡[w]\mathbb{Z}[w] associated to R~​(w)\tilde{R}(w) obtained by multiplication by the denominator of the coefficients.

5.1 Complexity of Rothstein-Trager Resultants

Let u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x) be in normal form with deg⁡a⁡(x)<n≔deg⁡b⁡(x)\deg a(x)<n\coloneqq\deg b(x), with the denominator b⁡(x)b(x) being square-free, height bounded by hh and multiplicative height at most H=2hH=2^{h}.

If we write b⁡(x)=∑i=0nbi​xib(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}x^{i} and a⁡(x)=∑i=0n−1ai​xia(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_{i}x^{i} then the Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)≔resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)\coloneqq\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) is the determinant of the (2​n−1)×(2​n−1)(2n-1)\times(2n-1) matrix

(bnan−1−n​w​bnbn−1bnan−1−n​w​bnbn−1⋱⋱⋱bna1−2​w​b2⋱b1bn−1a0−w​b1a1−2​w​b2an−1−n​w​bnb0b1a0−w​b1⋱b0⋱⋱⋱⋱b1⋱a1−2​w​b2b0a0−w​b1).\begin{pmatrix}b_{n}&&&&a_{n-1}-nwb_{n}&&&&\\ b_{n-1}&b_{n}&&&\vdots&a_{n-1}-nwb_{n}&&&\\ \vdots&b_{n-1}&\ddots&&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&&\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&b_{n}&a_{1}-2wb_{2}&\vdots&&\ddots&\\ b_{1}&\vdots&&b_{n-1}&a_{0}-wb_{1}&a_{1}-2wb_{2}&&&a_{n-1}-nwb_{n}\\ b_{0}&b_{1}&&\vdots&&a_{0}-wb_{1}&\ddots&&\vdots\\ &b_{0}&\ddots&\vdots&&&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&\ddots&b_{1}&&&&\ddots&a_{1}-2wb_{2}\\ &&&b_{0}&&&&&a_{0}-wb_{1}\end{pmatrix}. (16)

From the form of this Sylvester matrix, we see that the degree of R⁡(w)R(w) is at most nn, and its coefficient of degree nn is res⁡(b⁡(x),b′​(x))\res(b(x),b^{\prime}(x)), up to a sign. The assumption that b⁡(x)b(x) is square-free ensures deg⁡(R⁡(w))=n\deg(R(w))=n. Concerning the height of R⁡(w)R(w) we prove the following estimate.

Proposition 5.2.

For any 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n the coefficient rkr_{k} of wkw^{k} in R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) satisfies the inequality

|rk|≤(nk)6−k/2H2​n−1(n+1)(n+k−1)/2nn/2(2n+1)k/2.|r_{k}|\leq\binom{n}{k}6^{-k/2}H^{2n-1}(n+1)^{(n+k-1)/2}n^{n/2}(2n+1)^{k/2}.
