The determinant is linear with respect to its columns, hence we can write the last columns of the matrix (16) each as the sum of a part with the coefficients of a⁡(x)a(x), and a part with the coefficients of b′​(x)b^{\prime}(x), and factor ww in each column it appears. See Example 5.4 below for an illustration. The problem of bounding the height becomes bounding a determinant of a particular shape with integer coefficients and estimating the number of terms for each power of ww that appears.

Example 5.4.

In the case n=2n=2, b⁡(x)=b0+b1​x+b2​x2b(x)=b_{0}+b_{1}x+b_{2}x^{2} and a⁡(x)=a0+a1​xa(x)=a_{0}+a_{1}x, the polynomial R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) can be expanded as follows

R⁡(w)\displaystyle R(w) =|b2a1−2​w​b20b1a0−w​b1a1−2​w​b2b00a0−w​b1|\displaystyle=\begin{vmatrix}b_{2}&a_{1}-2wb_{2}&0\\ b_{1}&a_{0}-wb_{1}&a_{1}-2wb_{2}\\ b_{0}&0&a_{0}-wb_{1}\end{vmatrix}
=|b2a10b1a0a1b00a0|−w⁡(|b22​b20b1b1a1b00a0|+|b2a10b1a02​b2b00b1|)+w2​|b22​b20b1b12​b2b00b1|\displaystyle=\begin{vmatrix}b_{2}&a_{1}&0\\ b_{1}&a_{0}&a_{1}\\ b_{0}&0&a_{0}\end{vmatrix}-w\left(\begin{vmatrix}b_{2}&2b_{2}&0\\ b_{1}&b_{1}&a_{1}\\ b_{0}&0&a_{0}\end{vmatrix}+\begin{vmatrix}b_{2}&a_{1}&0\\ b_{1}&a_{0}&2b_{2}\\ b_{0}&0&b_{1}\end{vmatrix}\right)+w^{2}\begin{vmatrix}b_{2}&2b_{2}&0\\ b_{1}&b_{1}&2b_{2}\\ b_{0}&0&b_{1}\end{vmatrix}

The main ingredient for our estimates is the following lemma known as Hadamard’s inequality [13, Thm. 16.6, p. 477].

Lemma 5.5.

Let MM be a n×nn\times n matrix over ℝ\mathbb{R}, with columns C1,…,CnC_{1},\dots,C_{n}, and coefficients bounded by B>0B>0. Then

|det(M)|≤‖C1‖​…​‖Cn‖|\det(M)|\leq||C_{1}||\dots||C_{n}||

where ‖C‖||C|| denotes the 22-norm of the vector C∈ℝnC\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Proof of Proposition 5.2.

Following the idea of using linearity presented in the Example 5.4, we can write each coefficient rkr_{k} as a sum of determinants. Those determinants have a left block of n−1n-1 columns with the coefficients of b⁡(x)b(x), and a right block of nn columns, each being either coefficients of a⁡(x)a(x) or coefficients of b′​(x)b^{\prime}(x). Note that the power of ww in front of such a determinant is equal to the number of columns corresponding to coefficients of b′​(x)b^{\prime}(x). We will use Hadamard’s inequality, Lemma 5.5, on each of these determinants, hence let us compute a sharper bound on the 22-norms of each possible column. A column C1C_{1} of coefficients of b⁡(x)b(x) has at most n+1n+1 nonzero coefficients, each bounded by H=exp⁡(h)H=\exp(h), hence ‖C1‖=(∑i=0nbi2)1/2≤(n+1)1/2​H||C_{1}||=\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq(n+1)^{1/2}H. Similarly, a column C2C_{2} of coefficients of a⁡(x)a(x) has at most nn nonzero coefficients, each bounded by HH, hence ‖C2‖≤n1/2​H||C_{2}||\leq n^{1/2}H. Finally, if C3C_{3} is a column of coefficients of b′​(x)b^{\prime}(x), then ‖C3‖≤(∑i=1n(i​bi)2)1/2≤(n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6)1/2​H||C_{3}||\leq\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}(ib_{i})^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\left(\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\right)^{1/2}H.

Let us take any 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, then the coefficient rkr_{k} of wkw^{k} in R⁡(w)R(w) is a sum of determinants, each of which consists of n−1n-1 columns of coefficients of b⁡(x)b(x), of n−kn-k columns of coefficients of a⁡(x)a(x) and of kk columns of coefficients of b′​(x)b^{\prime}(x), and there are (nk)\binom{n}{k} such determinants. Each of these has the same upper bound given by ‖C1‖n−1​‖C2‖n−k​‖C3‖k||C_{1}||^{n-1}||C_{2}||^{n-k}||C_{3}||^{k}. Combining this and the bounds above on those norms concludes the proof. ∎

Knowing its height, we can estimate the complexity of computing the Rothstein-Trager resultant.

Proposition 5.6.

The Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) can be computed using O~​(n3​h)\tilde{O}(n^{3}h) bit operations.

Proof.

The coefficient of xn−1x^{n-1} in a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x)a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x) cannot vanish hence degx⁡(a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))=n−1\deg_{x}(a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x))=n-1. By Proposition 5.2, the height HRH_{R} of the Rothstein-Trager polynomial satisfies log⁡(HR)=O~​(n​h)\log(H_{R})=\tilde{O}(nh). Thus taking a prime p>2​HRp>2H_{R}, knowing the Rothstein-Trager resultant in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w] allows us to uniquely reconstruct it in ℚ⁡[w]\mathbb{Q}[w]. Corollary 11.21 from [13] states we can compute this polynomial in 𝔽p​[w]\mathbb{F}_{p}[w] in O~​(n2)\tilde{O}(n^{2}) operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, each with a cost O~​(log⁡(p))\tilde{O}(\log(p)), thus in total we can compute R⁡(w)∈ℚ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Q}[w] by performing O~​(n3​h)\tilde{O}(n^{3}h) bit operations. ∎

Taking the square-free part of the Rothstein-Trager resultant can alter its height, let us bound the height of any of its factors.

Proposition 5.7.

Any factor of R⁡(w)=resx⁡(b⁡(x),a⁡(x)−w⋅b′​(x))R(w)=\res_{x}(b(x),a(x)-w\cdot b^{\prime}(x)) has height at most

22​n+1π​n⋅H2​n−1⋅(n+1)2​n.\frac{2^{2n+1}}{\pi n}\cdot H^{2n-1}\cdot(n+1)^{2n}.
Proof.

Let HRH_{R} be the height of R⁡(w)≔rn​wn+⋯+r0R(w)\coloneqq r_{n}w^{n}+\dots+r_{0}. Let ‖R⁡(w)‖2=(∑k=0n|rk|2)1/2\|R(w)\|_{2}=\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}|r_{k}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}. Assume P⁡(w)∈ℤ⁡[w]P(w)\in\mathbb{Z}[w] is a factor of R⁡(w)R(w), Theorem 2 in [31] ensures that for the height HPH_{P} of P⁡(w)P(w) we have

HP≤max((ℓk), 0≤k≤ℓ≤n)∥R(w)∥2.H_{P}\leq\max\left(\binom{\ell}{k},\ 0\leq k\leq\ell\leq n\right)\|R(w)\|_{2}.

We have naïvely ‖R⁡(w)‖2≤(n+1)1/2​HR\|R(w)\|_{2}\leq(n+1)^{1/2}H_{R}. The maximum for fixed ℓ\ell is the central binomial coefficient (ℓ⌊ℓ/2⌋)\binom{\ell}{\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor}, which is an increasing sequence of ℓ\ell, thus HP≤(n⌊n/2⌋)​(n+1)1/2​HRH_{P}\leq\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(n+1)^{1/2}H_{R}. Combining this with Proposition 5.2 we obtain HP≤(n+1)2​n​(n⌊n/2⌋)2​H2​n−1H_{P}\leq(n+1)^{2n}\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}^{2}H^{2n-1}. The following upper bound on the central binomial coefficient yields the announced result

(n⌊n/2⌋)≤2n+1/2π​n.\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\leq\frac{2^{n+1/2}}{\sqrt{\pi n}}.

If nn is even this is a classical result, let us prove that it holds for any odd n∈ℕ≥3n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}. We have

(nn−12)=(n−1n−12)+(n−1n−32)≤2n−1/2π⁡(n−1)⋅(1+n−1n+1).\binom{n}{\frac{n-1}{2}}=\binom{n-1}{\frac{n-1}{2}}+\binom{n-1}{\frac{n-3}{2}}\leq\frac{2^{n-1/2}}{\sqrt{\pi(n-1)}}\cdot\left(1+\frac{n-1}{n+1}\right).

The result follows by dividing by the desired bound and using that x↦12​(xx−1)1/2​(1+x−1x+1)x\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)^{1/2}\left(1+\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right) attains its minimum 3​34​2<1\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\sqrt{2}}<1 on [2,+∞)[2,+\infty) at x=3x=3. ∎

Remark 5.8.

Starting from u⁡(x)≔a⁡(x)b⁡(x)∈ℚ¯​(x)∖ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\coloneqq\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\setminus\mathbb{Q}(x), the computations are more costly. Indeed, in a number field ℚ⁡(α)=ℚ⁡[t]/(πα​(t))\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)=\mathbb{Q}[t]/(\pi_{\alpha}(t)) with πα​(t)∈ℚ​[t]\pi_{\alpha}(t)\in\mathbb{Q}[t] the minimal polynomial of α∈ℚ¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, elements are polynomials of degree smaller than deg⁡(πα​(t))\deg(\pi_{\alpha}(t)), hence algebraic number multiplication has the complexity of modular polynomial multiplication.

5.2 Complexity Estimates for Finding Rational Roots of the Rothstein-Trager Resultant

In Section 3.1 we noted algebraicity of the solutions of (2) can be decided by Algorithm 1. We briefly investigate the complexity of this algorithm. For efficiently finding all the rational roots of a polynomial we have the following complexity [7, Prop. 21.22].

Theorem 5.9.

Let R⁡(w)∈ℤ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Z}[w] be a square-free, primitive polynomial of degree nn and height hRh_{R}. The computation of all rational roots of R⁡(w)R(w) can be performed, in O~​(n2​hR)\tilde{O}(n^{2}h_{R}) bit operations.

Remark 5.10.

Von zur Gathen and Gerhard only give a probabilistic algorithm performing the task in the same expected complexity [13, Thm. 15.21]. The algorithm described in [7] uses a deterministic (potentially costly) algorithm to find roots of the polynomial modulo a deterministically defined small prime number, and then lifts them to characteristic zero. It improves a result by Loos [28], who proposed a deterministic algorithm for finding rational roots in O~​(n3​h)\tilde{O}(n^{3}h) bit operations.

Using the corresponding algorithm the cost of computing the Rothstein-Trager resultant is comparable to finding rational roots, see Proposition 5.6. We obtain the following Corollary.

Corollary 5.11.

Given u⁡(x)≔a⁡(x)b⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\coloneqq\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\in\mathbb{Q}(x) of degree nn and height hh, deciding if all solutions of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) are algebraic can be done by performing O~​(n3​h)\tilde{O}(n^{3}h) bit operations.

5.3 Computation of the Bound on the Primes

Given u⁡(x)u(x), and having computed the Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)∈ℤ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Z}[w], Theorem 1.2 gives an explicit bound σ∈ℕ\sigma\in\mathbb{N} on the number of pp-curvatures to check, depending on rnr_{n}, the leading coefficient, on ΔR≔resw⁡(R⁡(w),R′​(w))\Delta_{R}\coloneq\res_{w}(R(w),R^{\prime}(w)), and on an upper bound BB on the modulus of all roots of R⁡(w)R(w).

An arbitrarily precise estimate of BB is possible without factoring completely the polynomial R⁡(w)R(w), for example by following ideas from an unpublished report of Schönhage in which an algorithm to find the complex roots of a polynomial R⁡(w)∈ℂ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{C}[w] with arbitrary precision is presented [45, Thm. 15.1].

Proposition 5.12 (Schönhage).

Let R⁡(w)∈ℤ⁡[w]R(w)\in\mathbb{Z}[w] of degree nn and τ>0\tau>0. The computation of B0>0B_{0}>0 such that the maximum modulus rr of all roots of R⁡(w)R(w) satisfies B0​e−τ<r<B0​eτB_{0}e^{-\tau}<r<B_{0}e^{\tau} can be done in O⁡(n2​(log⁡(1τ)+log⁡(log⁡(n)))​log⁡(4τ))O(n^{2}(\log(\frac{1}{\tau})+\log(\log(n)))\log(\frac{4}{\tau})) binary operations.

The bound BB we are looking for is B0​eτB_{0}e^{\tau}. For estimating the complexity of Algorithm 3, we will see that simply taking τ=1/2\tau=1/2 suits us, hence the complexity of computing the bound BB is O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) bit operations.

Of course, instead of computing a bound BB this way, one could use a classical bound depending only on the coefficients of R⁡(w)R(w), like B≤1+maxi⁡|rirn|B\leq 1+\max_{i}\left|\frac{r_{i}}{r_{n}}\right|, as we will do in the proof of our complexity estimates to bound σ\sigma. In practice, however, such a bound is usually much less tight.

5.4 Checking the Vanishing of pp-Curvatures

Our goal in this section is to explain how to efficiently check if the pp-curvatures of equation (2) vanish. We recall that the pp-curvature of equation y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x), is u(p−1)​(x)+u​(x)pmodpu^{(p-1)}(x)+u(x)^{p}\bmod p. Consider now u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x) of degree n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and multiplicative height at most H>0H>0.

To compute pp-curvatures we rely on an algorithm due to Bostan and Schost [9] which is tailored specifically for first-order differential equations. By ‘‘computing’’ a pp-curvature, we mean that we compute enough terms of its Taylor expansion in order to uniquely reconstruct it knowing a bound on the degrees of its numerator and denominator. Indeed, a rational function with numerator’s and denominator’s degrees at most nn is completely determined by nn and the first 2​n2n coefficients of its Taylor series expansion. In [9, Theorem 2], Bostan and Schost compute the pp-curvature starting from a differential equation over 𝔽p​(x)\mathbb{F}_{p}(x), while we want as input a coefficient in ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x), thus we cannot apply directly their result.

Proposition 5.13 (Bostan, Schost).

Let u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x) of degree n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, with coefficients bounded by H>0H>0. For any prime number pp the computation of the pp-curvature of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) can be performed in O~​(n2​log⁡(p)2+n​log⁡(H))\tilde{O}(n^{2}\log(p)^{2}+n\log(H)) bit operations, where we neglect factors log⁡(n)\log(n) and log⁡(log⁡(p))\log(\log(p)).

The computation of all pp-curvatures of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) for p≤Sp\leq S can be done in O~​(n2​S​log⁡(H)/log⁡(S)+n​S​log⁡(S))\tilde{O}(n^{2}S\log(H)/\log(S)+nS\log(S)) bit operations.

Proof.

What we wish to do is first reduce a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x) modulo pp, and then compute the pp-curvature. We need to perform O⁡(n)O(n) reductions modulo pp, one for each coefficient of a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x). With Euclidean divisions each of them can be done in O~​(log⁡(p)+log⁡(H))\tilde{O}(\log(p)+\log(H)) bit operations. We then refer to [9, Theorem 2] to ensure that from this point the pp-curvature can be computed in O~​(n2​log⁡(p))\tilde{O}(n^{2}\log(p)) operations in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, thus O~​(n2​log⁡(p)2)\tilde{O}(n^{2}\log(p)^{2}) bit operations and we obtain the announced complexity for computing one pp-curvature. The complexity of computing the pp-curvatures for all primes up to SS follows from the Prime Number Theorem ∑p≤S1=O⁡(S/log⁡(S))\sum_{p\leq S}1=O(S/\log(S)) and the estimate ∑p≤Slog⁡(p)2=O⁡(S​log⁡(S))\sum_{p\leq S}\log(p)^{2}=O(S\log(S)). ∎

Remark 5.14.

An efficient algorithm to compute the characteristic polynomials of the pp-curvatures for any order differential equations for all primes p≤Sp\leq S simultaneously in O~​(S⁡(log⁡(H)+n)​nω+1)\tilde{O}(S(\log(H)+n)n^{\omega+1}) bit operations is given by Pagès in [37], where ω<2.3728596\omega<2.3728596 is an exponent for matrix multiplication. This is easily adapted to check the nilpotence of the pp-curvatures in the same complexity. Checking nullity in such a complexity could prove crucial in the development of efficient algorithms for a potential effective version of the Grothendieck pp-curvature conjecture for (classes of) higher order equations.

5.5 Complexity Estimate

Our algorithm to decide the nature of all solutions of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) by computing pp-curvatures is presented above in Algorithm 3.

Proposition 5.15.

We have

δ⁡(ΔR)<4(log⁡2)2​((2​n−1)2​log⁡(H)+4​n2​log⁡(n+1)+log⁡(24​n2−13n/2​(π​n)2​n−1))2.\delta(\Delta_{R})<\frac{4}{(\log 2)^{2}}\left((2n-1)^{2}\log(H)+4n^{2}\log(n+1)+\log\left(\frac{2^{4n^{2}-1}}{3^{n/2}(\pi n)^{2n-1}}\right)\right)^{2}. (17)

In particular, with the notations as above, we have δ⁡(ΔR)=O~​(n4​(log⁡H+log⁡n)2)\delta(\Delta_{R})=\tilde{O}(n^{4}(\log H+\log n)^{2}).

Proof.

The statement can be deduced by applying a bound on the size of coefficients of the factors of the Rothstein-Trager resultant, Proposition 5.7, and then Proposition 5.2 to compute a bound on ΔR\Delta_{R}: first we compute a bound on the height of R⁡(w)R(w), the square-free part of the Rothstein-Trager resultant of a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x), and use a bound on the height of its Rothstein-Trager to obtain a bound for its leading coefficient, which is precisely ΔR\Delta_{R}. We conclude using Lemma 5.16, below. ∎

Lemma 5.16.

Let Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in\mathbb{N} and δ=∏p|Δp1/(p−1)\delta=\prod_{p|\Delta}p^{1/(p-1)}, then δ⁡(Δ)≤4log⁡(2)2​log⁡(Δ)2\delta(\Delta)\leq\frac{4}{\log(2)^{2}}\log(\Delta)^{2}.

Proof.

First we remark that if ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N} is such that ℓ​#≤Δ<(ℓ+1)​#\ell\#\leq\Delta<(\ell+1)\#, then δ⁡(Δ)≤δ⁡(ℓ​#)\delta(\Delta)\leq\delta(\ell\#) where ℓ​#≔∏p≤ℓp\ell\#\coloneqq\prod_{p\leq\ell}p is the primorial of ℓ\ell. This follows from the fact that x1/(x−1)x^{1/(x-1)} is decreasing for x≥2x\geq 2. We will now estimate δ⁡(ℓ​#)\delta(\ell\#). In [41, Theorem 10], we find that for ℓ≥557\ell\geq 557, we have 0.92⋅ℓ≤log⁡(ℓ​#)0.92\cdot\ell\leq\log(\ell\#). Checking

ℓ≤2log⁡(2)​log⁡(ℓ​#)\ell\leq\frac{2}{\log(2)}\log(\ell\#) (18)

numerically for 1≤ℓ≤5571\leq\ell\leq 557 we conclude that ℓlog⁡(ℓ​#)\frac{\ell}{\log(\ell\#)} attains its maximum for ℓ=2\ell=2, i.e., (18) holds for all ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. Moreover, we have the estimate log⁡(δ⁡(ℓ​#))=∑p≤ℓlog⁡(p)p−1≤2​∑p≤ℓlog⁡(p)p≤2​log⁡(ℓ)\log(\delta(\ell\#))=\sum_{p\leq\ell}\frac{\log(p)}{p-1}\leq 2\sum_{p\leq\ell}\frac{\log(p)}{p}\leq 2\log(\ell) following [41, Eq. (2.5), (2.11)], hence δ⁡(ℓ​#)≤ℓ2\delta(\ell\#)\leq\ell^{2}. Taking now ℓ\ell such that ℓ​#≤Δ≤(ℓ+1)​#\ell\#\leq\Delta\leq(\ell+1)\# we obtain

δ⁡(Δ)≤δ⁡(ℓ​#)≤ℓ2≤(2log⁡(2)​log⁡(ℓ​#))2≤4log⁡(2)2​log⁡(Δ)2.∎\delta(\Delta)\leq\delta(\ell\#)\leq\ell^{2}\leq\left(\frac{2}{\log(2)}\log(\ell\#)\right)^{2}\leq\frac{4}{\log(2)^{2}}\log(\Delta)^{2}.\qed
Proposition 5.17.

Given u⁡(x)≔a⁡(x)b⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\coloneqq\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\in\mathbb{Q}(x) of degree nn and multiplicative height HH, deciding if all solutions of y′​(x)=u⁡(x)​y​(x)y^{\prime}(x)=u(x)y(x) are algebraic can be done using Algorithm 3 by performing O~​(Δb6​B)=O~​(H12​n−6​n12​n​3−3​n)\tilde{O}(\Delta_{b}^{6}B)=\tilde{O}(H^{12n-6}n^{12n}3^{-3n}) bit operations, where O~\tilde{O} hides factors polynomial in nn and logarithmic in HH.

Proof.

We compute R⁡(w),Δb,R(w),\Delta_{b}, and a bound on δ\delta as described in the algorithm, and the maximal modulus of a root of R⁡(w)R(w), up to a constant factor by for instance setting τ=12\tau=\frac{1}{2} in Proposition 5.12. This we will use as an upper bound on BB. With this we obtain an upper bound on σ\sigma. Clearly the complexities of these computations are negligible compared to the computation of sufficiently many pp-curvatures as described below.

By Theorem 1.3, it suffices to compute the pp-curvatures up to σ\sigma, defined in its statement, not dividing Δb\Delta_{b}. Checking for a single prime pp, whether pp divides Δb\Delta_{b} can be performed in O⁡(log⁡(Δb))O(\log(\Delta_{b})) bit operations, for all primes up to Δb\Delta_{b} naïvely in O~​(Δb),\tilde{O}(\Delta_{b}), where logarithmic factors in Δb\Delta_{b} are again neglected.

We set S=σS=\sigma in Proposition 5.13. In accordance with Proposition 5.15 the contribution of δ\delta in the size of σ\sigma is negligible and we have σ=O~​(B​Δb6)\sigma=\tilde{O}(B\Delta_{b}^{6}), where we omit logarithmic factors in Δb\Delta_{b}. Cauchy’s bound on the roots of R⁡(w)=rn​wn+⋯+r0R(w)=r_{n}w^{n}+\dots+r_{0} states that we can take BB at most 1+maxi⁡|rirn|1+\max_{i}\left|\frac{r_{i}}{r_{n}}\right|, hence σ=O~​(Δb5​HR)\sigma=\tilde{O}(\Delta_{b}^{5}H_{R}), where HRH_{R} denotes the multiplicative height of R⁡(w)R(w). Using estimates from Proposition 5.2 to estimate this height and Δb\Delta_{b} we find both Δb\Delta_{b} and HRH_{R} to be in O~(H2​n−1n2​n−1/23−n/2)\tilde{O}(H^{2n-1}n^{2n-1/2}3^{-n/2}). Taking the 66-th power of this quantity and combining with Proposition 5.13 concludes. ∎

We warn the reader that the multiplicative height HH appearing is exponential in the height hh appearing in other complexity estimates.

This finishes the proof of the complexity estimates in Theorem 1.3. Note that Algorithm 3 delays the computation of BB and σ\sigma, to after checking some amount of pp-curvatures. This does not affect the complexity estimates presented here, but allows the algorithm to finish quickly for many examples, in which it returns transcendental.

Our algorithm is to be compared with the Algorithm 1 based on finding rational roots of a polynomial, whose complexity is polynomial in the degree and linear in the height as stated in Corollary 5.11. This is vastly smaller than our exponential bounds in the degree nn and height hh to verify algebraicity. However, we expect rational functions yielding transcendental solutions to have pp-curvatures that do not vanish for very small primes already, allowing Algorithm 3 to conclude much faster than Algorithm 1. Making an assumption as described above on the maximal expected first non-vanishing pp-curvatures gives a heuristic about the differences in complexity in practice. This general behavior is highlighted on examples in the following section.

Remark 5.18.

As highlighted already in Remark 5.8, our algorithm extends to the case of u​(x)∈ℚ¯​(x)∖ℚ​(x)u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\setminus\mathbb{Q}(x), however the complexity estimate of Proposition 5.17 does not hold because computations are more costly in number fields.

6 Implementations

6.1 Algorithmic Improvements

The following paragraphs discuss our implementation of Algorithm 3 in SageMath, that is available on GitHub with examples: https://github.com/plucas0/Honda.git.

The crucial algorithmic idea of the design of Algorithm 3 is to delay the moment when costly computations are done, that is the computation of the Rothstein-Trager resultant R⁡(w)R(w), when the degree of the input increases. By checking the ‘‘first’’ pp-curvatures, in our implementation for primes pp up to Δb\Delta_{b}, we try to return ‘‘Transcendental’’ before having to compute R⁡(w)R(w). In case no pp-curvature vanishes until this point, the computation of further pp-curvatures, potentially up to σ\sigma, is inevitable and this has much higher complexity than the computation of R⁡(w)R(w). When computing the bound BB on the modulus of the roots of R⁡(w)R(w), the precision τ\tau of the computation influences the complexity, see Proposition 5.12. In our case, computing all pp-curvatures up to σ\sigma already exceeds the capabilities of modern computers in most cases. For theoretical estimates, having BB multiplied by a constant factor does not change the complexity of the computations. Our implementation relies on native SageMath functions numerically computing zeroes of a polynomial, up to a fixed precision of 2−532^{-53}.

The naïve computation of δ⁡(ΔR)\delta(\Delta_{R}) can be costly, as it relies on the factoring of large integers. Using the bound obtained in (17) we avoid the computation of ΔR\Delta_{R}, an iterated resultant, and its prime factors. However, this bound appears to be highly non-optimal on examples. In our implementation we thus decide to compute ΔR\Delta_{R} and try for a small number of primes (up to T=1009T=1009) to find its contributions to δ⁡(ΔR)\delta(\Delta_{R}). There remains Δ~R\tilde{\Delta}_{R}, the product of its large factors, whose contribution to δ⁡(ΔR)\delta(\Delta_{R}) is bounded from above by Tv/(T−1)T^{v/(T-1)} for v=logT⁡(Δ~R)v=\log_{T}(\tilde{\Delta}_{R}).

Finally, the theoretical complexity of reducing polynomials modulo many primes pp simultaneously can be improved by adapting algorithms of polynomial multi-point evaluation for integers. However this is not done in our implementation, and reduction mod pp does not have a significant impact on computation time compared to the other operations performed by the algorithm.

Remark 6.1.

The delaying of the computation of the full Rothstein-Trager resultant is not as easily possible if u​(x)∈ℚ¯​(x)∖ℚ​(x)u(x)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\setminus\mathbb{Q}(x) as explained in Remark 5.1, and we do not know a method to delay this computation. For this reason, our implementation only treats the case of u⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡(x)u(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(x).

6.2 Competing Algorithms

6.2.1 Computation of pp-curvatures

First of all we would like to ensure and to convince the reader that our implementation of the algorithm from [9] to compute pp-curvatures of first-order differential equations is indeed faster than Pagès’ implementation of his algorithm [37] applied to first-order equations. The following timings in average were noted for both algorithms when asked to compute pp-curvatures for primes up to SS on random polynomial inputs a⁡(x),b⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]a(x),b(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] of given multiplicative height HH and degrees n−1n-1, respectively nn.

We see that for ‘‘small’’ inputs Bostan and Schost’s algorithm is faster than Pagès’ algorithm, and this remains the case when increasing any parameter.

6.2.2 Maple’s istranscendental

The maple package gfun [44] has a command called istranscendental based on the algorithms described in [8], aiming to prove transcendence of a given solution of a given differential equation. Among other things, it checks whether the singularities of the minimal differential operator annihilating a given function are all regular, and if its local exponents are rational. This is a necessary criterion for the algebraicity of the solution, so in case one of these conditions is violated, the command outputs true. For first-order differential equations however, Proposition 3.3 ensures that the conditions are also sufficient for algebraicity. While istranscendental outputs FAIL in this case, we can actually conclude algebraicity and thus we are (ab)using the command as an implementation of Algorithm 2.

6.2.3 Rational Roots of the Rothstein-Trager resultant

In Section 5.2 we investigated the theoretical complexity of Algorithm 1 which decides algebraicity of the solutions of (2) by checking whether the Rothstein-Trager resultant of the coefficient u⁡(x)u(x) completely factors over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. This is equivalent to checking that the number of its rational roots is equal to its degree, as the algorithm describes. For this purpose, SageMath’s native roots command performs a full factorization in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x], while Maple has more efficient methods implemented. We will see in the timings in the next section, that the computation of the resultant is the computationally more complex task in practice.

6.3 Examples

6.3.1 Small Inputs

Tests of our implementation of Algorithm 3 on very small examples, with small inputs and algebraic output, quickly reach the limits of modern computers’ capabilities, as displayed in Table 2. We also compare our algorithm (pp-curv) with istranscendental (ist) and the computation of the Rothstein-Trager resultant and its rational roots (RR) in Maple, and with computation of the resultant and performing its full factorization (fact) in SageMath.

In particular, on the last line, it takes approximately 11 minute to compute pp-curvatures for primes pp up to 2⋅1052\cdot 10^{5}, an extrapolation indicates it would take more than 22 years to compute them all up to σ≈1011\sigma\approx 10^{11}. At the same time it is obvious that the polynomial x2−4x^{2}-4 splits in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x], hence we would like to return ‘‘Algebraic’’ instantly.

6.3.2 Large Random Inputs

Certifying algebraicity using our approach is difficult. Both the theoretical complexity and the timings of our algorithm suggest so, already for small degree and height of the input. Proving transcendence, however, is in general much easier as we expect that in this case – except for very specific polynomials – the pp-curvatures for some small primes pp will not vanish. This might seem counterintuitive when compared to numbers – for which proving transcendence is considered hard – but this behavior was already observed in the functional context in [8]. By ‘‘small’’, we mean that we expect that it suffices to check a number of pp-curvatures significantly smaller than the bound σ\sigma of Theorem 1.3, but the latter is, to our knowledge, the best proven bound. Thus, in practice, our algorithm should be viewed rather only as a semi-algorithm in the sense that if the output is algebraic the algorithm will not terminate in reasonable time, except in very specific examples. The observed behavior worsens as the input degree and height increase, hence let us focus on the case where the output is transcendental. Note that testing pp-curvatures up to some (arbitrarily chosen) bound and returning ‘‘Transcendental’’ when one does not vanish is possible without relying on our Theorem 1.3, one only needs to know the ‘‘bad primes’’, cf. Proposition 2.5.

It is expected that the solution of a first order differential equation with coefficient u⁡(x)=a⁡(x)/b⁡(x)u(x)=a(x)/b(x) for integer polynomials a⁡(x),b⁡(x)a(x),b(x) of fixed degree n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} with random integer coefficients in [−H,H][-H,H], for H∈ℕ>0H\in\mathbb{N}_{>0} is transcendental, and checking that is possible by computation of very few pp-curvatures. In Table 3, computation times of all algorithms mentioned in Section 6.2, including Algorithm 3, are compared on inputs consisting of two such polynomials, with the first polynomial’s degree strictly smaller than the second’s. The algorithms we compare are our implementation of Algorithm 3 in SageMath (pp-curv), Maple’s istranscendental (ist), computing the Rothstein-Trager resultant (RT) and using Maple’s roots command for finding the rational roots of this resultant (RR), and computing the Rothstein-Trager resultant in SageMath and factoring it (fact). Of course the last algorithm is expected not to be competitive, still we display the timings to have a comparison in SageMath, the same system as our implementation.

The timings are given for random inputs a⁡(x),b⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]a(x),b(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] of multiplicative height at most HH and degree n−1n-1, respectively, nn, where Algorithm 3 returns ‘‘Transcendental.’’ The tests for degrees up to 4040 were performed on samples of hundreds of random rational functions, the size of the sample for the tests in degree 8080 and 160160 were respectively 100100 and 1010. In all our experiments, we observed that most examples return transcendental after computing a non-vanishing pp-curvature with pp no greater than 1717. In such cases, we avoid the computation of the Rothstein-Trager polynomial and only compute its leading coefficients, resx⁡(b⁡(x),b′​(x))\res_{x}(b(x),b^{\prime}(x)), whereas the factorization approach cannot take this shortcut.

The timings of computing Rothstein-Trager resultants separately were only performed in Maple, which outperforms SageMath on this task. We observe that the time for finding all rational roots of the resultant is negligible compared to computing the resultant in the first place, and that our implementation outperforms any algorithm requiring the computation of the resultant. The timings nicely illustrate, that for generic examples our algorithm returns ‘‘Transcendental’’ quickly, as claimed at the end of Section 5.5.

One can hand-craft examples on which we need to test relatively large primes pp – at least compared to the generic behavior. In the case of a quadratic polynomial, this smallest prime for which it does not factor into a product of two linear factors is the smallest quadratic non-residue in its splitting field. Examples of quadratic fields with prescribed least quadratic non-residue can be found in [30]. From this one can construct coefficients u⁡(x)u(x) of differential equations, for which the first prime for which the pp-curvature does not vanish is comparatively large. For instance, if a⁡(x)=1a(x)=1, b⁡(x)=x2−3818929b(x)=x^{2}-3818929, the prime p=2p=2 divides Δb=res⁡(b⁡(x),b′​(x))\Delta_{b}=\res(b(x),b^{\prime}(x)), and for all other primes up to 4343 the pp-curvatures vanish, but not the 4747-curvature. Our algorithm runs in 8080 milliseconds on this example.

More generally, we already discussed the connection of our problem with bounding the least prime that does not split in a number field in Section 3.

A systematic construction of polynomials R⁡(w)R(w) with ‘‘large’’ smallest prime pp for which the reduction of R⁡(w)R(w) does not split completely, or of coefficients u⁡(x)u(x) of differential equations for which the first non-vanishing pp-curvature is high, is not known to us.
